query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin hafnium coating onto the surface of a refractory high‐entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature oxygen resistance by generating a continuous, dense HfO₂ scale that retards oxygen diffusion and subsequent degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a V–Zr–Hf–Nb–Ta or similar alloy) that, without intervention, forms non-protective oxides and suffers significant weight gain and surface degradation under high-temperature oxidation.
generation.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin hafnium coating on the alloy surface using a high-temperature compatible method.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at a high temperature for a prolonged period to simulate extreme operational conditions typical of high-temperature structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The hafnium coating reacts preferentially with oxygen to form a conformal, adherent HfO₂ layer that adheres strongly to the alloy substrate.
generation.mechanism: The rapid oxidation of hafnium forms a stable and slow-growing HfO₂ barrier that limits further oxygen ingress. This scale suppresses additional oxidation of the underlying alloy matrix, thereby preserving the alloy’s structural integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated samples, the hafnium-coated alloy will show a significantly lower weight gain (indicative of reduced oxidation) and a visibly intact, dense oxide scale after high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit substantial oxidation weight gain, surface degradation (e.g., dents, pulverization), and formation of non-protective scales when exposed to 1000 °C in air for extended durations.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the Hf coating is expected under static, high-temperature (around 1000 °C) oxidizing conditions. Its performance under severe thermal cycling or mechanical stress needs further investigation.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness, long-term adhesion under cyclic thermal conditions, and potential interactions with the underlying alloy microstructure remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical refractory HEA samples. Apply the optimized hafnium coating to one group and leave the other group uncoated. Expose both groups to air at 1000 °C for 50 hours.
measurements: Monitor and record the weight gain per unit area for both coated and uncoated samples.
Conduct surface and cross-sectional SEM/EDS analyses to assess the morphology, integrity, and continuity of the oxide scales.
Perform mechanical testing (e.g., hardness or tensile strength) post-oxidation to compare degradation levels between the two sets.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hafnium-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain, or if SEM/EDS analyses reveal a discontinuous or non-protective HfO₂ layer (comparable to or worse than that on uncoated samples), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application.
